sections.heading: Asking you to keep my love alive
sections.text: Lord Jesus, if I truly love you, I will want to look for you and be near you. But I know I cannot even keep that desire alive on my own. Keep my love for you from cooling off. Teach me to seek you because you are good, and because every real good I need is found in you.
theological_themes: Love for Christ is itself sustained by Christ’s grace.
The soul seeks Christ because he is good and is the source of true good.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitful life with him depends on abiding in him, not on self-generated strength. This grounds the prayer’s confession that even seeking and loving Christ must be sustained by him.
John roots human love for God in God’s prior love. The prayer’s desire to love Jesus does not treat love as self-produced but as a response awakened by grace.

sections.heading: Coming to you though I do not deserve to be welcomed
sections.text: You would be right not to pay attention to me. I am sinful, self-centered, and far smaller than I pretend to be. Yet I still come looking for you. And when you let me find you, I do not meet consuming anger. I meet mercy. You stand between me and the judgment I deserve, like a great rock giving shade in unbearable heat. Because I belong to you, I can live sheltered in your love.
theological_themes: Human unworthiness and selfishness are real and must be confessed honestly.
Christ shelters his people from wrath and receives them in mercy.
The believer’s safety rests in Christ, not in personal worthiness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects Christ’s death for sinners with being saved from God’s wrath through him. This directly supports the prayer’s image of Christ standing between the believer and deserved judgment.
Isaiah uses the image of a sheltering refuge and shade in a weary land. The prayer draws on that biblical pattern to speak of Christ as protection and relief for the soul.

sections.heading: Admitting what I become without you
sections.text: When my mind runs ahead without you, it weaves lies and convinces me they are true. When my desires move without you, even the things that look religious can be lifeless. I need you to live in me and keep me close to you. I do not have the kind of sight that can grasp you by nature. I live by faith in you—the One I cannot yet see, but whose glory is brighter to me than anything in this world.
theological_themes: Apart from Christ, human reasoning and desires are corrupted by sin.
Religious activity without Christ can be spiritually dead.
The Christian life is lived by faith in the unseen but glorious Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Christian life as walking by faith rather than by sight. This supports the prayer’s confession that the believer depends on faith in Christ rather than natural spiritual perception.
Peter speaks to believers who love and trust Christ though they do not see him now. That fits the prayer’s focus on loving the unseen Christ whose glory outshines all else.

Hebrews describes Christ’s blood cleansing the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. This helps explain the prayer’s concern that activity apart from Christ, even if outwardly religious, is spiritually empty.

sections.heading: Giving you all the glory
sections.text: When I see how much sin is still in me, let me admit that the shame is mine. And when I see anything good, let me know where it comes from: all goodness is in you, and all glory belongs to you. Do not let me dress up my pride as spirituality. Strip away every excuse I use to claim credit for what only your grace can do.
theological_themes: Sin and shame belong to the sinner, while all true good comes from Christ.
God receives the glory for salvation and holiness.
Humility means refusing to take credit for grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul’s confession that nothing good dwells in his flesh reflects the prayer’s honest view of remaining sin. It supports the distinction between what belongs to the sinner by nature and what must come from God.

Paul teaches that Christ himself is the believer’s righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so boasting belongs only in the Lord. This grounds the prayer’s insistence that all good and glory are Christ’s.

sections.heading: Learning to recognize true grace
sections.text: Keep me from thinking you are most present just because I feel something unusual or impressive inside me. Do not let me mistake a strange brightness in my heart for the real work of grace. Show me that your clearest work is often this: you make my own glory grow dim, and you make the honor, pleasure, and success of this world lose their power over me. Let your glory rise before me until everything else looks small. Make me poor in spirit. Help me find my treasure, my safety, and my good in you.
theological_themes: Spiritual experiences must be tested by whether they exalt Christ rather than the self.
True grace humbles the believer and weakens the world’s grip.
Christ’s glory outshines creation and becomes the believer’s true good.

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts former gains as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This supports the prayer’s request that worldly honor and pleasure be eclipsed by Christ’s glory.
Jesus blesses the poor in spirit, those who come empty-handed before God. This illuminates the prayer’s desire to be humbled rather than impressed with personal spiritual experience.
Paul boasts only in the cross, through which the world is crucified to him and he to the world. This fits the prayer’s longing for Christ to eclipse personal glory and worldly goods.

sections.heading: Resting everything in you
sections.text: So teach me to distrust myself in the right way—not with despair, but with clear eyes. Let me stop treating myself as my refuge, wisdom, or righteousness. Let me see that everything I need is in you, and let me gladly live from your fullness. Amen.
theological_themes: Self-distrust is not despair but humility before Christ.
Christ is the believer’s sufficient wisdom, righteousness, refuge, and life.

scripture_references.connection: This passage calls God’s people to trust the Lord rather than lean on their own understanding. It supports the prayer’s request for a humble distrust of self and a settled reliance on God.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers have been filled in him. This directly grounds the final request to find one’s all in Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase “as one elect” reflects a Reformed doctrine of election. I preserved the substance by speaking of belonging to Christ and being sheltered in his love, without expanding the prayer into a full doctrinal statement on election.

The warning about “some strange light” is a critique of mistaking unusual inward experiences for genuine grace. This can be doctrinally and pastorally sensitive because Christian traditions differ in how they evaluate spiritual experiences; the adaptation keeps the focus on biblical discernment: true grace exalts Christ and humbles the self.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the image of Christ standing between the scorching sun and the soul as Christ sheltering the believer from deserved judgment, because the original immediately contrasts wrath with sweet love.
I rendered “no natural eyes to see thee” as the need to live by faith rather than natural spiritual perception, rather than as a denial that creation or conscience can bear any witness to God.
I treated “all sin is in me” as an unsparing confession of indwelling sin, not as a claim that the believer is nothing but sin or lacks any work of grace.
I interpreted the final request to “distrust myself” as humble reliance on Christ rather than psychological self-hatred or despair.
